## Context
Which way each handler fails — closed, loud, or quiet — is the load-bearing design
decision of this plugin, and `CLAUDE.md` devotes a section to it. It is stated in three places that
must agree and are not checked against each other: the module docstring (`hook.py:16–22`), each
handler's own `try/except` (`:121–140`, `:390–397`, `:446–477`, `:545–560`, `:649–656`, `:696–703`,
`:820–829`), and `main()`'s last-resort `if event == "guard"` / `if event == "inject"` chain
(`:854–891`). A new event means remembering all three, and nothing fails if you don't.

## Why it matters
`verify.py` has to reach past the interface to test it: `:186` and `:286` build Python
source in a string (`crash_snippet = "import sys, hook\n…"`) to monkeypatch `hook.read_payload` and
`hook._read_text`, because there is no seam at which a failing input can be injected. That is the
"testing past the interface" smell — the module is the wrong shape for the test that matters most.

## Proposed change / acceptance criteria
- [ ] Make the policy the value in the existing `EVENTS` table:
`{"guard": (event_guard, FailClosed), "inject": (event_inject, FailLoud), …}`. Handlers compute a
decision or raise; the dispatch seam owns fail-closed, fail-loud and fail-quiet. `main()`'s `if
event ==` chain becomes a lookup, and the contract becomes assertable directly — one check per row —
instead of via two embedded source strings.

## Context
"Pull one field out of the payload without trusting the whole thing to parse" is
stated four times: `_PROMPT_FIELD_RE` (`hook.py:443`), `_COMMAND_FIELD_RE` (`:537`),
`_LAST_MESSAGE_FIELD_RE` (`:777`) and `_FILE_PATH_RE` (`:601`), plus two extractor functions
(`_guard_subject` `:540`, `_extract_file_path` `:611`) and one inline `m.group(0)` (`:809`). The
comment at `:775` says as much: *"Same shape as `_COMMAND_FIELD_RE`"*.

## Why it matters
The fourth silently differs. Three match the raw JSON slice and allow backslash-escaped
quotes (`(?:[^"\\]|\\.)*`); `_FILE_PATH_RE` captures the value with `([^"]*)` and drops escape
handling. Nothing currently exercises a Windows path with an escaped quote in it, so the divergence
is unobserved rather than proven harmless.

## Proposed change / acceptance criteria
- [ ] One `field_slice(payload, name)` at that seam, with raw-slice-vs-value as a
parameter. `guard`'s deliberate three-tier ladder — field absent means fall back to matching the
whole payload — moves inside it and gets tested once instead of being re-derived per handler.

## Context
`hook.py:271–397` is one 127-line function doing five things: parse the
`.claude/standards` override, scan depth-1 for markers, rescan from the parent when the project root
is a Unity `Assets/` folder, assemble English grammar (`"One"`/`"Two"`, plural, verb — `:346–369`),

- The rescan at `:309–314` retypes the detection loop from `:293–299` verbatim rather than calling

## Context
`verify.py`'s executor and archivist shape checks fail if either agent sets
`hooks:`, `mcpServers:` or `permissionMode:`, on the stated grounds that "plugin subagents
silently ignore" them — the reasoning being that a field which reads as configuration and does
nothing is worse than no field. The current subagent reference documents `permissionMode` (and
`hooks`, `mcpServers`, and several others: `disallowedTools`, `maxTurns`, `skills`, `memory`,
`isolation`, `background`, `color`) as **supported** frontmatter fields.

## Why it matters
Noticed while establishing that `effort:` is a documented frontmatter field, during
the 2.18.0 delegation-visibility work. Both checks were read at that commit; neither was changed,
because the claim they encode was not re-verified either way and changing a passing check on the
strength of a docs page would swap one unverified assertion for another.

## Proposed change / acceptance criteria
- [ ] Establish, per field and on a surface this plugin actually claims, whether
it is honoured for a *plugin-shipped* agent — which is not the same question as whether it is
honoured for a user-level `~/.claude/agents/` one, and the distinction is the whole basis of the
existing check. Then either narrow the forbidden list to the fields that really are inert, or
keep it and record the evidence next to it. A third possibility is that the answer differs by
field, in which case the check needs per-field reasoning rather than one list.

**What this is (plain version)**

Every plan longer than three steps gets turned into issues before any work starts: one issue for the whole plan, and one small issue for each step inside it, written so you can follow them without reading code. Each step follows the same loop, and nothing is closed until you have tried it and said so. The same change also replaces the single all-purpose helper with three cheaper tiers of helper, so the work costs less.

**The loop for every step**
1. Take the next open step (your new issues go first).
2. Mark it "in progress".
3. Do the work on a branch.
4. Write what changed and the real test results on the issue.
5. Open a pull request that links the issue but does not close it.
6. Stop and ask you to test.
7. Only after you approve: close the issue, then move to the next step.

New work found along the way becomes its own issue instead of being slipped in.

**Decisions already made**
- Claude may add the "in progress" label to an existing issue and take it off when the issue closes.
- One issue per plan or major change; smaller issues for the steps, in plain language.
- Pull requests link with "Refs #N", never "Closes #N", so GitHub cannot close an issue before you have tested.

**Still to decide**
- Whether code edits are blocked until a plan's issues exist, or only reminded.
- Whether the three helper tiers are approved as thin definition files.
- Which repos this applies to.

Full design, Focus Deck flow and cost measurements: `docs/plans/issue-workflow-and-tiered-subagents-proposal.md` (on the branch `claude/hooks-efficiency-review-32732b`, pull request 106).

Related older issues: #94, #103, #105 (the same ideas, written before the design existed).

Steps are listed as separate issues that say "Part of" this one.

Part of #107. Related to #110, which covers approved plans; this is the case that never reaches plan approval.

**What happened** (Ajw2003/RockSkipping, 2026-09-30). In one session Claude built two multi-step pieces of work: a party UI (lobby QR layout, in-match HUD, leaderboard, final-scores screen) and a set of four bug fixes. It created no issues for the UI work until the owner asked "why aren't you actively creating git issues for these?". It also left fixed issues open with a vague "close whichever look right" instead of asking which to close, never used the `in progress` label, and never added `Claude completed this` when closing. Claude agreed it was a mistake. A per-project memory now records it, but the owner wants this enforced everywhere by the plugin, not remembered per project.

**Why the rule didn't stop it.** `issue-workflow.md` is clear, but the only thing that arms the `commitgate` hook is `delegate` on `PostToolUse` `ExitPlanMode`. This session planned in chat (clarifying questions, then a plan written to `docs/plans/`) and never used plan mode, so `house-rules-issues.json` was never written and `commitgate` never blocked a source edit. Anything planned outside plan mode skips the whole workflow without a sound.

**Proposed changes**
1. **Arm the gate on multi-file source work, not only on `ExitPlanMode`.** For example, `commitgate` could count distinct source files edited since the last labelled issue was created, and block after a threshold (say a third file) until a parent and a child issue exist for the current work. "Two labelled issues exist somewhere in the repo" should not count: in this session older open issues would have satisfied that check.
2. **Recognise plans written to `docs/plans/*.md`** (numbered steps) as the same trigger as an approved plan.
3. **Lifecycle reminders at `Stop`.** If a turn committed work that references an open issue (`Refs #N`), the reply must end by asking which named issues the owner has tested and wants closed, not leave it open-ended. If an issue was worked on without `in progress`, or closed without `Claude completed this`, say so.
4. **Close via a confirmed question.** When the owner confirms in chat, close each issue with the confirming comment and apply `Claude completed this`. That was skipped here too.

**Done when:** in a test repo, starting a three-file change with no plan mode is blocked until a parent and child issue exist. Committing work with `Refs #N` ends the turn with a concrete close question naming the issues. Closing applies `Claude completed this` and removes `in progress`.

body:
**What this is (plain version)**

Any background job Claude starts (a helper, a long command) gets checked every 5 minutes to see whether it has stopped making progress. The check must be as cheap as possible and must give a reliable yes or no.

**The test**

A helper writes a new line to its transcript file for every message and tool call; a background command does the same to its output file. If that file has not changed for 5 minutes, the job has made no progress. That is one file-age check: no model call and no parsing. A small script, `stallcheck.py`, does it and prints `ok`, `STALLED` or `finished` per job. It is built and tested (70 ms per run) on branch `claude/stallcheck`.

**How it runs for free**

`python stallcheck.py --watch` loops every 30 seconds inside the Monitor tool and prints a line only when a job stalls or finishes. Claude is woken only then, so a healthy 40-minute job costs no tokens. Waking Claude every 5 minutes instead costs a full conversation read each time.

**Known limit**

A long model call or a usage-limit wait writes nothing either, so it reads as STALLED. That is the definition of stalled here; the response to a STALLED line is to look at why, not to assume the job died.

**Steps**
1. The script and its tests (script done; tests and the rest below to do).
2. Change the reminder hooks that say "check in every 10 minutes" to 5 minutes, naming the exact `stallcheck.py` command and the Monitor way to run it.
3. Rules text, detail file, docs and version bump.

Steps 2 and 3 wait until the helper-tiers pull request (#111, #112) is merged, because both change the same hook file.

Refs #120.

**What happened (2026-10-01, PlunderSpell):** a builder subagent was blocked in a wait loop with no time limit for about 12 minutes, and not productive for about 20. `stallcheck.py --watch` printed STALLED for it twice in that time, and only because a message I sent wrote to its transcript and briefly flipped it to ok. **Fix:** while a job stays STALLED, re-print it every threshold period (e.g. at 300 s, 600 s, 900 s), with the stall age growing. Add a test: one STALLED transcript left untouched across 3 periods produces 3 lines.

2. Report it to the user with the age and what it is blocked on.
3. If it is a command that can't finish, ask to stop that command.
4. Never cite "no STALLED line since" as evidence of progress.
5. Never rely on SendMessage to unstick an agent blocked inside a tool call.

## What happens

A background builder's command hits a house-rules approval prompt, and the builder sits blocked until the owner notices. On 2026-10-02, in Ajw2003/PlunderSpell, this happened three times:

| Builder | Command that prompted | Time blocked |
|---|---|---|
| nav graph (PlunderSpell #221) | `rm -f` of its own uncommitted draft file | about 20 min |
| guard core (PlunderSpell #206) | `python - <<'PY' ...` heredoc that wrote a section into a docs file | 20+ min, still waiting when this was filed |
| co-op settings (PlunderSpell #199, 2026-09-30) | `git checkout -- ProjectSettings.asset` | about 1 hour |

The stall check catches it: it prints `STALLED` every 5 minutes. But all it says is "no new activity", so the parent has to open the transcript to find out it's a pending prompt rather than a hang. The owner, meanwhile, may be away from the machine.

This isn't project-specific. Any project using the builder agent will hit it.

## Why

- **The prompts:** the PreToolUse hook prompts on deletes, on scripted file writes (a heredoc into python, `sed -i`, `cat >`) and on git restore/checkout.
- **What builders do:** they often reach for those forms instead of the Write/Edit tools.
- **No way out:** a background subagent can't answer a prompt or route around it.

## Suggested fixes

1. **Builder agent definition** (`agents/builder.md`):
   - write and edit files with the Write/Edit tools, never shell scripts;
   - never `rm`; list files that should be deleted in the report instead;
   - never `git checkout`, `git restore` or `git stash`.
2. **`stallcheck.py`:**
   - when the agent's last transcript entry is a `tool_use` with no matching `tool_result`, print something like `STALLED ... waiting on tool call: <first 80 chars of the command>`, so the parent knows straight away it's a pending prompt;
   - optionally flag that the parent should push-notify the owner.
3. **`hook.py` STALLED guidance:** tell the parent to check for a pending prompt first, and to push-notify once (not every 5 minutes) when it finds one.

Related: #134 (helpers on their own branches stop for approval on every commit) is the same family of problem, for commits.

body:
## What happens

Handover cards for Windows often start a program with PowerShell's call operator:

```powershell
& "<absolute path>\some-tool.exe"
```

aj reports this form "always breaks, never works". It is the form the house rules themselves teach: `docs/example-environment.md` ("The `sh` trap") gives `& "C:\Program Files\Git\bin\sh.exe" path/to/script.sh`.

## Why it is fragile

- **`&` only means "run this" in PowerShell.** In `cmd.exe` it is a command separator, so a line starting with `&` fails there. The Run button does not pick the shell from the fence label (`claude-house-rules/plugins/house-rules/rules/detail/handover-command.md`, item 2, observed 2026-09-07), so a `powershell` card can still be run by something that is not PowerShell.
- **Dropping the `&` silently does nothing in PowerShell.** A quoted path on its own is just a string and gets printed back, not run. Checked in PowerShell 7.4.6 (Linux): `"/usr/bin/true"` printed `/usr/bin/true`; `& "/usr/bin/echo" x` and an unquoted `/usr/bin/echo x` both ran.
- **When it does fail, the error is misleading.** PowerShell reports "is not recognized as the name of a cmdlet…", which reads like a syntax problem. In the most recent case (RockSkipping, 2026-10-02) the real cause was that the exe was not in the folder at all (an earlier step had checked out the wrong commit). The `&` was blamed for that.

The `cmd.exe` behaviour above is standard cmd semantics but was not run here: the session that wrote this has no Windows.

## What would fix it

Options, for aj to choose:

1. **No `&` when the path has no spaces.** An unquoted absolute path runs the same in PowerShell and `cmd.exe`.
2. **For paths with spaces, a form that works in both shells,** for example `cmd /c` with the quoted path, or `Start-Process -Wait -NoNewWindow`. Each needs testing on a real Windows machine first.
3. **Add a `Test-Path` line before the launch,** so a missing file reports "not found" instead of looking like a syntax error.
4. **Update `docs/example-environment.md` and `rules/detail/handover-command.md`** to whichever form is chosen, so cards stop copying the old one.

body:
## What happened

A builder subagent (Ajw2003/PlunderSpell, issue #236, 2026-10-02) started a Unity client build and then waited for it with a hand-written poll loop:

```bash
for i in $(seq 1 100); do sleep 5; s="$(unity command build_status --no-banner --format json 2>/dev/null)"; case "$s" in *'"completed"'*|*'"failed"'*) break;; esac; done
```

The build finished in 19 s (`result: Succeeded`, 0 errors), but the loop never matched and ran its full cap of 100 passes, roughly 10 minutes of dead time. stallcheck then reported the agent STALLED, which looked like a hang to the owner and prompted two manual check-ins.

## Why it never matched

The Unity CLI's `--format json` wraps the command's own result as a **JSON string inside the JSON envelope**, so every inner quote is escaped:

```
"result": "{\"status\":\"completed\",\"buildId\":\"build_b6e1df119b49\"
```

`"completed"` never appears in the text; only `\"completed\"` does. Checked against the live output: the pattern `*'"completed"'*` prints "does NOT match" while the build is complete. The same envelope shape comes back from `recompile_status`, `test_status` and other `unity command` status calls, so any wait written this way can only end by timing out.

## Proposed fix

1. A rule for builder and executor prompts (next to #125): never detect a state by grepping or `case`-matching raw CLI JSON. Parse it (`python -c "import json..."`, decoding `data.result` a second time when it is a string), or call a project helper that does.
2. A rule that every wait must confirm its success condition can fire: run the check once against a known-finished state (or the current one) and see it match, before entering the loop. This is the "a wait's target is real and one status check shows it working" house rule applied to the match pattern itself, not only the process.
3. Optionally, have stallcheck name the long-running tool call (for example "inside one Bash call for 9 min") so a stuck wait reads differently from a stuck agent.

Related: #125 (waits with no time limit), #85 (verify a wait's target before leaving it), #127 (stallcheck false STALLED).

## What happened

In Ajw2003/PlunderSpell (#238, 2026-10-02), a builder subagent was asked for one in-game co-op measurement before its fix and one after. It made **8 co-op runs**, three of them within six minutes. Each run opens Play mode in the Editor plus a second game window on the owner's screen. The runs were mostly spent fixing its own measuring script: an eval compile error, a harness that pushed the player nowhere, and extra diagnostics added run after run. The owner, at the keyboard, asked "too many tests back to back, what's happening?" and the parent had to message the builder to stop.

The owner's standing rule for that project is one check run per change, with repeats only to chase a named flaky failure. Builders never see a project's memory, so the rule only reached this builder if the parent happened to paste it into the prompt.

## The gap

`plugins/house-rules/agents/builder.md:13` limits **test suites** ("run the full suites exactly once, at the end") but says nothing about **in-game, end-to-end or harness runs** (co-op checks, play-mode drives, capture scripts, benchmark runs). Those are the slowest and most visible checks, and the ones a builder is most tempted to repeat while debugging its own harness.

## Proposed rule (for builder.md, so every builder carries it)

> **One run per check.** Any in-game, end-to-end or harness check (a play session, a co-op run, a capture script, a benchmark) runs once after the change, plus once before it if the task asks for a before/after. If the check itself misbehaves (a harness bug, a setup that does not reach the state under test), stop and report what failed. Do not edit the harness and run again. A repeat is allowed only to chase a specific, named flaky failure, and the report says why. Every run counts in the report: "N runs, why each".

A matching line could also go in the delegate-execution rule detail, so a parent writing a builder prompt knows the builder already carries this and does not need to restate it.

## Related

#125 (waits with no time limit), #138 (waits that can never match), #120 (checking background jobs).

Follows #108 and #109.

## What went wrong

On 2026-10-03, Ajw2003/PlunderSpell had 28 issues whose work was finished and tested, but all of them were still open. The owner closed them in one sweep (see Ajw2003/PlunderSpell#246). Nothing in the issue loop ever asked whether to close them.

The rule (`rules/detail/issue-workflow.md`) says:
- step 5: PR bodies say `Refs #N`, never a closing word, so GitHub never closes an issue at merge;
- step 6: "Closing an issue always asks."

Step 5 is enforced by a hook. Step 6 only says what happens *if* a close is attempted. Nothing makes the ask happen, so turning off GitHub's auto-close left no closing path at all. Other things made it worse:

1. **The work sat on one long branch.** 186 commits were never merged, and no PR existed until the sweep. "Merged PR link" (step 6) never existed to point at.
2. **Status went into the docs, not the issues.** `docs/3-state/ProjectState.md` said "#207 is in" while #207 stayed open.
3. **Step 4's `in progress` label was mostly not applied**, so the board couldn't show what was underway either.
4. **Sessions ended mid-work** (usage limit, handoffs), before any end-of-issue step could run.
5. **Parent issues don't close** when their last child does.

## Proposed change

Add an end-of-issue step to the loop, enforced the same way step 5 is:

1. **Done means ready to test.** When an issue's "Done when" is met (tests or runs quoted), I add a `ready to test` label, comment with the commits and the evidence, and ask the owner in the same session: "#N is done: <one line>. Close it now, or after you've tested?" Closing still needs the owner's yes.
2. **A Stop-hook check.** At turn end, if commits in this session reference `#N` and #N is open with neither `ready to test` nor a recorded "not done" reason, the hook reminds me to do step 1. (Same reminder shape as the docs-tier check.)
3. **The state doc and the issue move together.** Whenever the state doc records "#N is in", the issue gets `ready to test` in the same turn.
4. **Parents follow children.** When the last child of a parent is closed or `ready to test`, ask about the parent too.
5. **Session start lists the test queue.** Next to the open-issue titles, list the issues labelled `ready to test`, so a backlog is visible at the start of every session instead of after two days.
6. **Step 6 wording.** The comment links the PR whether or not it has merged, and says which branch the work is on if it isn't on `main`.

## Done when

- The rule text in `rules/house-rules.md` and `rules/detail/issue-workflow.md` has the end-of-issue step. `verify.py` checks that the two copies agree.
- The Stop-hook check fires in a test session that commits `#N` work without labelling #N, and stays quiet once #N is labelled or closed.
- Session start shows the `ready to test` list.

- the builder's final report, once it finished.

Nothing in between. The builder's own tool calls and commits don't appear in the parent conversation. The stall watch (`stallcheck.py --watch`) prints only `STALLED` or `finished` lines, and its 5-minute threshold fires falsely during long single commands (a Unity test run or build), so a "stalled" line is the only mid-build signal and it is often wrong. This sits against the house rule "Never hide work: it stays visible, reachable and readable ... on mobile too".

## What the owner wants

To see, from the phone, what a running builder is doing: which step of its plan it is on, what it last finished (a commit, a test total, a check's PASS/FAIL), and whether it is waiting on something.

## Ideas (not decided)

1. **Builders post checkpoints.** The builder agent definition tells the builder to send the parent a one-line progress message at each step boundary (step started, commit pushed, test totals, check result). The parent relays it as a short visible line, or as a push notification to the phone.
2. **A progress file the parent watches.** The builder appends one line per checkpoint to a file under the project's `docs/` (or the session scratchpad); the parent runs a `Monitor` on it, so each line becomes a visible event in the conversation without a model call per line.
3. **A better stall watch.** Make `stallcheck.py` also report the builder's last tool name and summary (for example "running run_tests.sh, 3 min"), so the 5-minute line says what it is doing instead of just `STALLED`.

Option 2 needs nothing from the platform and fits the existing Monitor pattern; option 1 is the most natural to read on a phone.

## Acceptance

With a builder running for 20+ minutes, someone following only on the mobile app sees at least one line per step of the builder's plan, each saying what finished, without the parent being asked.

aj's request: destructive actions are permitted only on a Claude-created branch, and only if the work is already saved somewhere the destructive action would not affect.

## Decided with aj (2026-10-07)

- **Safe case:** on a `claude/` branch, with nothing uncommitted or untracked (`git status` clean) and every commit already on a remote. A destructive step goes ahead there without asking.
- **Everything else:** ask first, exactly as today (say what's lost, run `git status`, wait for a yes).
- **Enforced by `guard`, not only the rule text.**

## Scope in `guard`

- **Unasked in the safe case:** `git reset`, `git revert`, `git rebase`, `git checkout --` and `git restore`. With a clean tree and everything pushed, each of these loses nothing that isn't on the remote.
- **Still prompts:**
  - force-push: it overwrites the remote, which is the "saved elsewhere" copy;
  - `git clean`: can remove ignored files that exist nowhere else;
  - `git stash drop/clear`: stashes are never pushed;
  - `rm`: guard can't tell where its target is saved;
  - `merge`, `cherry-pick`, `am`, `apply`, `filter-branch`: covered by the separate rule against finishing an operation aj started.

body:
## What happened

In a PlunderSpell session (2026-10-08, working through Ajw2003/PlunderSpell#368), the owner stepped away while Claude was mid-merge. Every Bash command ran in a sibling worktree (`PlunderSpell-lair`, where the Unity Editor was open), outside the session folder, so Claude Code asked permission for each one. Once one prompt went unanswered for 5 minutes, the #142 timer hook:

1. refused it,
2. refused **every later prompt at once** ("another prompt already went unanswered … refused at once instead of waiting again"), and
3. told Claude never to retry that action, or a variation of it, for the rest of the session.

What got stopped this way, none of it destructive or unrecoverable:
- running a test script (`Tools/Unity/coop_lair_check.sh`, a co-op check that plays in a throwaway save slot and restores settings)
- a Unity `eval` that only read `isPlaying`
- adding a `Today.md` note and committing and pushing on a `claude/` branch
- a `git merge -s ours` on a `claude/` branch the agent had just created (adds a commit, changes no files)
- `gh pr create` to `main` (opening a PR is reviewable and reversible; only *merging* to main should need the owner)
- `request_directory` to add the worktree to the session

The session stalled for about an hour across three "carry on" messages. Once the owner was back at the PC, every one of those actions ran fine; the co-op check passed.

## What the owner wants (their words, paraphrased)

> A refusal shouldn't block testing or the next steps unless there is no way around an action being destructive and unrecoverable. Opening a PR to main shouldn't be blocked, only merging it into main. A co-op check is a testing file: why is it raising a permission prompt at all?

## Proposed change

- **Only destructive, unrecoverable actions get a timeout refusal**: delete, force-push, `reset --hard`, killing processes, merging to `main` or a branch that isn't a `claude/` branch, closing issues and PRs, deleting branches. Anything else that times out should be let through (or never prompt at all), not refused.
- **No cascade.** One unanswered prompt must not turn later prompts into instant refusals, and "never retry this session" should apply only to the destructive class.
- **Fewer prompts in the first place.** Test and check scripts under the project's `Tools/` folder, Unity CLI read-only calls, `gh pr create`, and plain commit, merge and push on `claude/` branches should be pre-allowed. That should hold in sibling git worktrees of the same repo too, not only in the session folder.
- The rule text (`rules/detail/destructive-action.md`, and the refusal message in `scripts/hook.py`) should say the same thing, so Claude doesn't treat a refused test run as off-limits.

## Done when
- [ ] A timed-out prompt for a non-destructive action (test script, PR create, commit or push on `claude/`) does not end up refused and does not block later prompts
- [ ] A timed-out destructive action is still refused and listed on the waiting list
- [ ] Project test scripts and `claude/`-branch git writes in a sibling worktree don't prompt
- [ ] Checked in a real desktop-app session with the owner away for over 5 minutes

Related: #142 (the timer this refines), #149, #159.

```

```

The attribution guard should have refused every one. It refused none. The agent then opened PRs #9 and #10 there with a "Generated with Claude Code" footer, which the guard never saw either.

## Why the guard missed the commits

Every commit set the author with a quoted value containing a space:

```
git -c user.name="aj's agent" -c user.email=... commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
```

`_GIT` in `scripts/hook.py` allows `-c` options, but matches each value with `[^\s]+`, which stops at the space inside the quotes. `_ATTRIBUTION_CMD_RE` then never sees `commit`, so the guard returns early. It never gets as far as checking the message text.

I checked this by loading `hook.py` and calling `_attribution_guard` directly, with the message carrying the Claude trailer in every case:

| Command form | Result |
|---|---|
| `git commit -m "..."` | DENIED |
| `git -c user.name=x commit -m "..."` | DENIED |
| `git -c user.name=aj -c user.email=a@b commit -F - <<EOF` | DENIED |
| `git -c user.name="aj's agent" commit -m "..."` | **ALLOWED** |
| `git -c user.name="aj's agent" -c user.email=a@b commit -q -F - <<EOF` (the form used) | **ALLOWED** |

The same `_GIT` prefix is shared by other git rules in `hook.py`, so this gap probably reaches past attribution: any guard keyed on a git subcommand can be stepped around the same way.

The cloud harness injects a reminder telling the agent to end every commit with `Co-Authored-By: Claude ...` and `Claude-Session: ...`, and every PR with "Generated with Claude Code". With no `attribution` setting in cloud sessions (#179) and the guard missing this command form, nothing caught it.

1. `_GIT` accepts quoted option values (`"..."` and `'...'`, spaces inside), with a test for each failing row above.
2. A test that the guard still denies when the author is set through `-c` with a space in the name, since that's exactly how "aj's agent" gets set.

3. "aj's agent **and others** added 6 commits": the "others" is the Claude co-author trailer still on older commits (#189).

## What was checked, and what it showed

**The footer is added after the agent sends the PR, and only on creation.**

- The agent created PR #11 through the GitHub MCP tool (`create_pull_request`) with a body ending in `---` and `Opened by AJ's agent`.
- Reading the PR back straight away showed a second `---` and an italic "Generated by Claude Code" line with a session link appended. The agent had not written it.
- Editing the body through the same tool (`update_pull_request`) without the footer **stuck**: the read-back ended at "Opened by AJ's agent". The edit path doesn't append it.
- Issue #189 here, created through the same MCP server (`issue_write`), has **no** footer. So issue creation doesn't append it either.

So the append happens on pull request creation only. The attribution guard can't stop it, even with #178 in place, because the text the agent sends is already clean.

**"with Claude" is not in the text at all.** GitHub shows it for any action taken with the Claude GitHub App's token, which is how cloud sessions reach GitHub. No wording change removes it. Only acting with a different token would, and a cloud session has no `gh` sign-in.

**What the guards did this session:**
- Creating a PR from a `claude/` branch was refused with the instruction to use `AjsAgent/<topic>`. Correct.
- A commit was refused because the identity read as Claude. **False alarm:** the global git config says Claude, but the repo's own `.git/config` sets `AJ's agent`, and `git var GIT_AUTHOR_IDENT` confirmed git would sign as `AJ's agent`. The guard seems to read the global value, or check from outside the repo.
- The first draft of this issue was refused because it quoted the trailer text it describes. **Second false alarm:** the guard can't tell text that adds the credit from text that reports it. This draft names the strings without spelling them out.

## What a fix needs

## What goes wrong (plain version)

The guard asks before risky shell commands. If the risky part is on the second line of a command, or comes after a tab, it isn't asked about at all.

These were run through the guard on 2026-10-09, on a branch that isn't the agent's:

| Command | Result |
|---|---|
| `rm -rf build` | asks |
| `ls` + new line + `rm -rf build` | **allowed** |
| `ls` + tab + `rm -rf b` | **allowed** |
| `ls &&` + new line + `rm -rf b` | **allowed** |
| `ls` + new line + `nohup x` | **allowed** |
| `ls` + new line + `setsid x` | **allowed** |
| `sleep 99 &` + new line + `ls` | **allowed** |
| `ls` + new line + `sleep 5 \| tail -1` | **allowed** |
| `ls` + new line + `git push --force` | asks (git patterns aren't affected) |

## Why it happens

The guard matches its patterns against the command as it sits inside the hook's JSON input (`_guard_subject` in `scripts/hook.py`), where a new line is the two characters `\n` and a tab is `\t`. The `rm`, `nohup`/`setsid`/`disown` and "wait piped to tail/head" patterns (`GUARD_R1` and `GUARD_R4`) require a non-letter just before the word. The `n` or `t` of the escape is a letter, so the pattern never matches. The trailing-`&` pattern only looks for `&` right before the closing quote, so `&` followed by a new line is missed too.

This has been true since the `rm` pattern was added in ab0cd02 (2026-09-11). It isn't a regression. Neither open branch changes it: Ajw2003/AjsClaudeCodeTools#190 (`AjsAgent/quoted-git-options`) and the `ccr-9ab94e76-iufs44` branch both keep the same patterns.

## What will be different

A risky command asks however it's laid out: on the first line, after a new line, after a tab, or after `&&` and a line break.

The smallest fix is to add `\\[nrt]` as an accepted "start" in each of those prefixes, for example `(^|\\[nrt]|[^0-9A-Za-z_./-])rm\s+\S`, and let the background-`&` pattern also end at `\\n`.

- `verify.py` has a case for each row above that is marked **allowed**, and each one now asks.

When aj's message contains an approval phrase (`Design approved`, `Build plan approved`, `QA passed/failed`, `skip design`) and the session folder is not inside a git repo, say so in one line: which folder was used, and that nothing moved.
